The state also will have significantly fewer students in our public schools. The Department of Finance projects a decline of 710,500 students from 2026 through 2036, and by the midpoint of this decline, we undoubtedly will see some major changes in the education structure.
This is only the beginning of the list of unknowns. Other questions include:
Will Californians still be paying billions of dollars per year for a nonfunctioning “high-speed” railroad system in 2031, rather than prioritizing schools for that spending?
Will taxpayers still be paying for ineffective programs that haven’t solved homelessness?
Will startups launch in California, or take their jobs and economic benefits to states with more competitive tax rates?
In short, it makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
What difference could five years make?
California’s finances can change substantially in a short period. Total state revenue for the current fiscal year is projected to be $21.5 billion higher than the amount collected five years earlier. The Department of Finance also recently reported that general fund revenue was running $5.5 billion above the projection used to draft the 2026-27 budget just six months earlier. This means the education funding guarantee will go up, too.
It makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
Timing is only one of the problems. While Proposition 3 is marketed as a “tax extension” that would only affect high-income residents, the truth is that it’s a major tax increase that would hit millions of small businesses as well as high-income individuals. The result: California’s affordability crisis gets worse.
The small-business aspect of Proposition 3 hasn’t received enough attention. California’s tax structure does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships, or S corporations that report business earnings on personal income tax returns.
This means the higher tax rates imposed by Proposition 3 would increase taxes on many small businesses, ultimately leading to higher prices for customers, fewer job opportunities for workers, or both.
ThePublic Policy Institute of California reported in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-businesses/) that sole proprietorships accounted for more than 3 million California businesses in 2023. But the number of those businesses whose owners would be impacted by Proposition 3 depends on their taxable income.
To the extent that Proposition 3 would hit high-income earners, it would make California more reliant on the most volatile source of revenue, while simultaneously making it even more volatile by giving high-income residents a new incentive to leave the state.
California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and would have a top personal income tax rate of 10.3% on income over $1 million without Proposition 3. The state also imposes a 1.3% State Disability Insurance tax on all income from salaries and wages, bringing the top tax rate to 11.6% on those forms of income, without Proposition 3.
As for the issue of an “extension” versus an “increase,” the fact is clear: If Proposition 3 is approved, Californians will pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more in state income tax than if the initiative is defeated (according to estimates by the Legislative Analyst’s Office). California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 3 would take the Prop 30 higher personal income tax rates on top earners and make them permanent. Voters approved Prop 30 as a temporary measure in 2012 to close a budget shortfall. The measure was then extended in 2016 under Prop 55. Under current law the increased taxes expire after the 2030 tax year, so a yes vote is, in effect, a tax increase from 2031 onward compared with the law as it now stands. Hoover Institution research on the 2012 rate increase found that high earners’ responses to the higher tax rates, either by leaving the state or reporting less income, erased much of the revenue the higher rates were expected to raise.
Other Hoover Institution research shows that California’s budget already depends to an unusual degree on a small, mobile group of taxpayers whose income tends to be dependent on stock market performance. It also finds that much of the money raised for schools has been absorbed by rising pension costs rather than reaching classrooms.
Proposition 3 would enshrine into the state constitution increased fiscal dependence on a variable tax with no future date for voters to revisit the decision.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0016).
Type: Initiative constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: The temporary higher personal income tax rates on top earners become permanent instead of expiring after the 2030 tax year. Taxable income above about $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers (2025 tax brackets, adjusted annually for inflation) would continue to face marginal rates of 10.3 to 12.3 percent and of 13.3 percent on income above $1 million.
A vote NO means: The higher tax rates expire on schedule. Beginning in 2031, the top rate would return to 9.3 percent (plus the separate 1 percent income tax surcharge on income above $1 million, for a combined top rate of 10.3 percent).
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0016, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf)
LAO analysis: Proposition 3, Legislative Analyst’s Office (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 3 would remove the expiration date on the higher personal income tax rates that California voters first approved as Proposition 30 in 2012. These temporary taxes were intended to forestall additional education budget cuts in the wake of tax revenue declines following the Great Recession. They were set to expire after 2018, but Proposition 55 in 2016 extended the taxes through 2030 and added the formula for the taxes to fund Medi-Cal when revenues exceed specific benchmarks.
Now Prop 3 would make these taxes—1, 2, and 3 percentage point surcharges on top of the state’s 9.3 percent bracket—permanent. Combined with the separate 1 percent surcharge tax on personal income above $1 million (created by Proposition 63 in 2004), the Prop 30 income tax surcharges give California the highest top marginal personal income tax rate in the nation, at 13.3 percent. This rises further to 14.6 percent on wage income once the now-uncapped state disability insurance payroll tax is included.
These income tax surcharges fall on roughly the top 2 percent of tax filers in any given year, a group that already pays about half of all state income taxes. Because much of their income comes from highly variable capital gains, stock options, and business sales, the Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) expects the revenue at stake to swing between about $5 billion in a weak year and $15 billion in a strong year.
Supporters stress that Proposition 3 does not raise anyone’s rate this year. That is true—but incomplete. Current law already schedules these rates to end after 2030, so the relevant comparison is not today’s tax bill but the one taxpayers would face in 2031. Measured against current law, a yes vote raises taxes on affected earners from that point forward, permanently. The LAO’s own description of a yes vote is that “an income tax increase on high-income earners” would become permanent.
Despite Prop 30 originally being advertised as necessary to avoid education funding cuts, the tax doesn’t provide as much additional state funding for schools as would be expected on the surface. The tax revenue flows into the state’s general fund and is held in the Education Protection Account (EPA), whereupon it is disbursed to schools (89 percent) and community colleges (11 percent). However, because the EPA counts as general fund revenue, and Prop 98 only mandates (under the formula currently in effect) that about 40 percent of the general fund goes to education, only about 40 percent of Prop 30’s tax revenue actually represents an increase to school funding. Except for special circumstances, the remaining 60 percent of the EPA doesn’t necessarily increase school-related expenditures because those dollars count toward the Prop 98 guarantee. This means that policymakers can use the funding to replace other obligatory general fund education expenditures on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
In years when the state’s general fund revenues exceed both the Proposition 98 education spending guarantee and the cost of maintaining existing state programs, half of the excess (up to $2 billion, as stipulated by Prop 55) goes to Medi-Cal health services. The remainder supports other general fund programs and budget reserves. In summary, what was initially framed as a temporary tax to avoid cuts to education funding has shifted to effectively become ordinary California tax revenue and is poised to become permanent.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0016, “The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0016%20%28%26quot%3BThe%20California%20Children%26%23039%3Bs%20Education%20and%20Health%20Care%20Protection%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (filed August 29, 2025).
Key language:
The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date for the higher tax brackets.
What it amends: Section 36 of Article XIII of the California Constitution, the section created by Proposition 30 and extended by Proposition 55. Because the change is constitutional, the legislature cannot repeal or reduce the rates—only another statewide vote could change the tax rates.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
A permanent extension of the 1, 2, and 3 percentage point personal income tax surcharges on high earners, which would otherwise expire after the 2030 tax year.
Where?
Statewide, written into the state constitution at Article XIII, Section 36.
When?
On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the rates never expire. If it fails, the last tax year of the higher rates is 2030.
Why?
The measure’s sponsors, led by the California Teachers Association, frame making the tax permanent as protecting school and children’s healthcare funding from what would otherwise be a revenue loss. Opponents, led by the California Taxpayers Association, argue that Californians already pay among the nation’s highest taxes and that Sacramento should fix its excessive spending before making temporary taxes permanent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
The LAO’s estimate that the Prop 30 income tax surcharge is worth from $5 billion to $15 billion in revenue is effectively a static figure: It assumes that high earners keep living, working, and reporting income in California exactly as they would without the tax. Hoover Institution research examines this assumption directly. Using the full dataset of California tax returns, Hoover Senior Fellow Joshua D. Rauh and coauthor Ryan Shyu studied what happened after Proposition 30 raised top rates in 2012—0.8 percent more of the top-bracket tax base left the state in 2013 than otherwise would have been expected without the tax change. Moreover, the high earners who stayed reported substantially less taxable income; counterintuitively, this was actually the larger effect. Together, these responses erased 45.2 percent of the expected revenue gain in the first year and 60.9 percent of the total gain within the first two years.
A companion Hoover analysis noted that the 2017 federal tax reform which created a cap on state and local tax deductions hit high-income Californians with a force equivalent to 82 percent of another Proposition 30 tax increase. It suggested that the state was likely on the wrong side of the Laffer curve, meaning that increasing the top income tax rates was actually reducing the total tax revenue collected.
Similarly, in an October 2026 op-ed on Proposition 3 itself, Rauh and Hoover fellow Gregory Kearney argue that the top-bracket tax rates are now money losers for California. Before the 2017 cap on state and local tax deductions, high-income Californians could deduct much of their state tax bill on their federal returns. This had the effect of softening the impact of the income tax surcharges. Once the cap took effect, the surcharges imposed by Prop 30 began bearing close to their full weight on the state’s high-income households, which sharpened the incentive to move or restructure income. By the authors’ estimates, since 2018 the state has been losing more tax revenue from departing taxpayers or erosion of the tax base than it collects from those that remain.
Supporters of Prop 3 reply that high earners have not fled California, pointing to studies that find modest migration among millionaires. But Rauh’s earlier findings show why that reply misses the point: Departures accounted for less than a tenth of the lost revenue. Most of the erosion came from taxpayers who stayed and reported less income. This could have occurred by realizing fewer capital gains, shifting business activity to other taxing jurisdictions, or simply working less (or perhaps accepting other forms of income). Effectively, Prop 30 has provided a textbook example of how a tax base can shrink without anyone moving away.
Proposition 3 would also enshrine a revenue structure that Hoover research identifies as a major source of California’s fiscal instability. Hoover Senior Fellow Lee E. Ohanian shows that the top 1 percent of California households now provides roughly 40 to 50 percent of all personal income tax revenue and that the top 10 percent pay almost 90 percent. Because high-earning households tend to receive a large portion of their income from the stock market, which is highly variable, California’s personal income tax revenue surged by 55 percent in 2021 and then fell nearly 35 percent in 2023.
This feast-or-famine paradigm creates complications for funding ongoing programs and exposes California to revenue risk that it has little control over. Rauh and coauthor Jillian Ludwig describe this fragility as “baked into the system” and recommend steering more capital gains revenue into reserves rather than ongoing spending. Proposition 3 does the opposite: It treats the most volatile revenue in the state as a permanent foundation for ongoing commitments.
Moreover, the phrase “the top 2 percent of tax filers” somewhat misrepresents who pays the Prop 30 income tax surcharges. This is because those who pay the tax are not solely a group of consistent high earners. Some Californians would cross the relevant tax threshold only in the year they sell a home they have owned for decades or a small business they built. Capital gains from home sales are taxable when they exceed the home-sale exclusion of $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for joint filers. Citing a 2025 Redfin analysis, Rauh and Kearney note that 62 percent of California homes have appreciated at least $250,000 in value over their last sale price, and 33 percent had appreciated by at least $500,000. This suggests that a sizable share of California homeowners would see large one-time gains that could push them into the surcharge brackets in the year they sell. Owners of pass-through businesses, who report business profits on their personal returns, would also face these surcharges in successful years or years where they sell their businesses.
The biggest argument made in favor of Proposition 3 is premised on public schools not losing existing funding. However, Hoover research raises the question of where the increased funding has actually gone. By Rauh and Kearney’s calculations, the annual pension contributions for California’s K–12 school districts almost tripled between 2015 and 2023 to about $13 billion (excluding teachers’ own contributions). Over that period, the share of school employee spending devoted to pensions nearly doubled, from about 7 percent to more than 13 percent. If school districts had held pension costs at their 2015 share, Rauh and Kearney estimate, nearly $6 billion more would have been available for other education priorities last year alone. In other words, Prop 30’s income tax surcharges appear to a large extent to be funding increased retirement benefits.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 3 would turn a tax that voters were told was temporary into a permanent feature of the California Constitution. Compared with current law, it raises taxes on high earners from 2031 onward. Hoover Institution research suggests the revenue it protects is considerably smaller than the official estimate because the state’s most mobile taxpayers respond to higher rates by leaving or by reporting less income. It would also lock in California’s reliance on a narrow and volatile tax base while doing nothing to address the pension costs that have absorbed much of the money raised in the name of schools.

PROP 3: The Permanent High-Income Tax Initiative
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%203.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Analysis & Assessment
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 3 would take the Prop 30 higher personal income tax rates on top earners and make them permanent. Voters approved Prop 30 as a temporary measure in 2012 to close a budget shortfall. The measure was then extended in 2016 under Prop 55. Under current law the increased taxes expire after the 2030 tax year, so a yes vote is, in effect, a tax increase from 2031 onward compared with the law as it now stands. Hoover Institution research on the 2012 rate increase found that high earners’ responses to the higher tax rates, either by leaving the state or reporting less income, erased much of the revenue the higher rates were expected to raise.
Other Hoover Institution research shows that California’s budget already depends to an unusual degree on a small, mobile group of taxpayers whose income tends to be dependent on stock market performance. It also finds that much of the money raised for schools has been absorbed by rising pension costs rather than reaching classrooms.
Proposition 3 would enshrine into the state constitution increased fiscal dependence on a variable tax with no future date for voters to revisit the decision.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0016).
Type: Initiative constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: The temporary higher personal income tax rates on top earners become permanent instead of expiring after the 2030 tax year. Taxable income above about $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers (2025 tax brackets, adjusted annually for inflation) would continue to face marginal rates of 10.3 to 12.3 percent and of 13.3 percent on income above $1 million.
A vote NO means: The higher tax rates expire on schedule. Beginning in 2031, the top rate would return to 9.3 percent (plus the separate 1 percent income tax surcharge on income above $1 million, for a combined top rate of 10.3 percent).
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0016, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf)
LAO analysis: Proposition 3, Legislative Analyst’s Office (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 3 would remove the expiration date on the higher personal income tax rates that California voters first approved as Proposition 30 in 2012. These temporary taxes were intended to forestall additional education budget cuts in the wake of tax revenue declines following the Great Recession. They were set to expire after 2018, but Proposition 55 in 2016 extended the taxes through 2030 and added the formula for the taxes to fund Medi-Cal when revenues exceed specific benchmarks.
Now Prop 3 would make these taxes—1, 2, and 3 percentage point surcharges on top of the state’s 9.3 percent bracket—permanent. Combined with the separate 1 percent surcharge tax on personal income above $1 million (created by Proposition 63 in 2004), the Prop 30 income tax surcharges give California the highest top marginal personal income tax rate in the nation, at 13.3 percent. This rises further to 14.6 percent on wage income once the now-uncapped state disability insurance payroll tax is included.
These income tax surcharges fall on roughly the top 2 percent of tax filers in any given year, a group that already pays about half of all state income taxes. Because much of their income comes from highly variable capital gains, stock options, and business sales, the Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) expects the revenue at stake to swing between about $5 billion in a weak year and $15 billion in a strong year.
Supporters stress that Proposition 3 does not raise anyone’s rate this year. That is true—but incomplete. Current law already schedules these rates to end after 2030, so the relevant comparison is not today’s tax bill but the one taxpayers would face in 2031. Measured against current law, a yes vote raises taxes on affected earners from that point forward, permanently. The LAO’s own description of a yes vote is that “an income tax increase on high-income earners” would become permanent.
Despite Prop 30 originally being advertised as necessary to avoid education funding cuts, the tax doesn’t provide as much additional state funding for schools as would be expected on the surface. The tax revenue flows into the state’s general fund and is held in the Education Protection Account (EPA), whereupon it is disbursed to schools (89 percent) and community colleges (11 percent). However, because the EPA counts as general fund revenue, and Prop 98 only mandates (under the formula currently in effect) that about 40 percent of the general fund goes to education, only about 40 percent of Prop 30’s tax revenue actually represents an increase to school funding. Except for special circumstances, the remaining 60 percent of the EPA doesn’t necessarily increase school-related expenditures because those dollars count toward the Prop 98 guarantee. This means that policymakers can use the funding to replace other obligatory general fund education expenditures on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
In years when the state’s general fund revenues exceed both the Proposition 98 education spending guarantee and the cost of maintaining existing state programs, half of the excess (up to $2 billion, as stipulated by Prop 55) goes to Medi-Cal health services. The remainder supports other general fund programs and budget reserves. In summary, what was initially framed as a temporary tax to avoid cuts to education funding has shifted to effectively become ordinary California tax revenue and is poised to become permanent.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0016, “The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0016%20%28%26quot%3BThe%20California%20Children%26%23039%3Bs%20Education%20and%20Health%20Care%20Protection%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (filed August 29, 2025).
Key language:
The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date for the higher tax brackets.
What it amends: Section 36 of Article XIII of the California Constitution, the section created by Proposition 30 and extended by Proposition 55. Because the change is constitutional, the legislature cannot repeal or reduce the rates—only another statewide vote could change the tax rates.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
A permanent extension of the 1, 2, and 3 percentage point personal income tax surcharges on high earners, which would otherwise expire after the 2030 tax year.
Where?
Statewide, written into the state constitution at Article XIII, Section 36.
When?
On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the rates never expire. If it fails, the last tax year of the higher rates is 2030.
Why?
The measure’s sponsors, led by the California Teachers Association, frame making the tax permanent as protecting school and children’s healthcare funding from what would otherwise be a revenue loss. Opponents, led by the California Taxpayers Association, argue that Californians already pay among the nation’s highest taxes and that Sacramento should fix its excessive spending before making temporary taxes permanent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
The LAO’s estimate that the Prop 30 income tax surcharge is worth from $5 billion to $15 billion in revenue is effectively a static figure: It assumes that high earners keep living, working, and reporting income in California exactly as they would without the tax. Hoover Institution research examines this assumption directly. Using the full dataset of California tax returns, Hoover Senior Fellow Joshua D. Rauh and coauthor Ryan Shyu studied what happened after Proposition 30 raised top rates in 2012—0.8 percent more of the top-bracket tax base left the state in 2013 than otherwise would have been expected without the tax change. Moreover, the high earners who stayed reported substantially less taxable income; counterintuitively, this was actually the larger effect. Together, these responses erased 45.2 percent of the expected revenue gain in the first year and 60.9 percent of the total gain within the first two years.
A companion Hoover analysis noted that the 2017 federal tax reform which created a cap on state and local tax deductions hit high-income Californians with a force equivalent to 82 percent of another Proposition 30 tax increase. It suggested that the state was likely on the wrong side of the Laffer curve, meaning that increasing the top income tax rates was actually reducing the total tax revenue collected.
Similarly, in an October 2026 op-ed on Proposition 3 itself, Rauh and Hoover fellow Gregory Kearney argue that the top-bracket tax rates are now money losers for California. Before the 2017 cap on state and local tax deductions, high-income Californians could deduct much of their state tax bill on their federal returns. This had the effect of softening the impact of the income tax surcharges. Once the cap took effect, the surcharges imposed by Prop 30 began bearing close to their full weight on the state’s high-income households, which sharpened the incentive to move or restructure income. By the authors’ estimates, since 2018 the state has been losing more tax revenue from departing taxpayers or erosion of the tax base than it collects from those that remain.

Most of the erosion came from taxpayers who stayed and reported less income. This could have occurred by realizing fewer capital gains, shifting business activity to other taxing jurisdictions, or simply working less (or perhaps accepting other forms of income). Effectively, Prop 30 has provided a textbook example of how a tax base can shrink without anyone moving away.
Proposition 3 would also enshrine a revenue structure that Hoover research identifies as a major source of California’s fiscal instability. Hoover Senior Fellow Lee E. Moreover, the phrase “the top 2 percent of tax filers” somewhat misrepresents who pays the Prop 30 income tax surcharges. Citing a 2025 Redfin analysis, Rauh and Kearney note that 62 percent of California homes have appreciated at least $250,000 in value over their last sale price, and 33 percent had appreciated by at least $500,000. This suggests that a sizable share of California homeowners would see large one-time gains that could push them into the surcharge brackets in the year they sell. Owners of pass-through businesses, who report business profits on their personal returns, would also face these surcharges in successful years or years where they sell their businesses.

By Rauh and Kearney’s calculations, the annual pension contributions for California’s K–12 school districts almost tripled between 2015 and 2023 to about $13 billion (excluding teachers’ own contributions). In other words, Prop 30’s income tax surcharges appear to a large extent to be funding increased retirement benefits.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 3 would turn a tax that voters were told was temporary into a permanent feature of the California Constitution. Compared with current law, it raises taxes on high earners from 2031 onward. Hoover Institution research suggests the revenue it protects is considerably smaller than the official estimate because the state’s most mobile taxpayers respond to higher rates by leaving or by reporting less income. Story Title:
Proposition 3: California doesn’t need another forever tax
October 28, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/voting10.jpg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/commentary-vote-no-proposition-3/769223). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.
Related Reading
CommentaryProposition 3 would help lock in hard-won resources for student well-being (https://edsource.org/2026/proposition-3-california-schools/769155) October 28, 2026
The state also will have significantly fewer students in our public schools. The Department of Finance projects a decline of 710,500 students from 2026 through 2036, and by the midpoint of this decline, we undoubtedly will see some major changes in the education structure.
This is only the beginning of the list of unknowns. Other questions include:
Will Californians still be paying billions of dollars per year for a nonfunctioning “high-speed” railroad system in 2031, rather than prioritizing schools for that spending?
Will taxpayers still be paying for ineffective programs that haven’t solved homelessness?
Will startups launch in California, or take their jobs and economic benefits to states with more competitive tax rates?
In short, it makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
What difference could five years make?
California’s finances can change substantially in a short period. Total state revenue for the current fiscal year is projected to be $21.5 billion higher than the amount collected five years earlier. The Department of Finance also recently reported that general fund revenue was running $5.5 billion above the projection used to draft the 2026-27 budget just six months earlier. This means the education funding guarantee will go up, too.
It makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
Timing is only one of the problems. While Proposition 3 is marketed as a “tax extension” that would only affect high-income residents, the truth is that it’s a major tax increase that would hit millions of small businesses as well as high-income individuals. The result: California’s affordability crisis gets worse.
The small-business aspect of Proposition 3 hasn’t received enough attention. California’s tax structure does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships, or S corporations that report business earnings on personal income tax returns.
This means the higher tax rates imposed by Proposition 3 would increase taxes on many small businesses, ultimately leading to higher prices for customers, fewer job opportunities for workers, or both.
ThePublic Policy Institute of California reported in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-businesses/) that sole proprietorships accounted for more than 3 million California businesses in 2023. But the number of those businesses whose owners would be impacted by Proposition 3 depends on their taxable income.
To the extent that Proposition 3 would hit high-income earners, it would make California more reliant on the most volatile source of revenue, while simultaneously making it even more volatile by giving high-income residents a new incentive to leave the state.
California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and would have a top personal income tax rate of 10.3% on income over $1 million without Proposition 3. The state also imposes a 1.3% State Disability Insurance tax on all income from salaries and wages, bringing the top tax rate to 11.6% on those forms of income, without Proposition 3.
As for the issue of an “extension” versus an “increase,” the fact is clear: If Proposition 3 is approved, Californians will pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more in state income tax than if the initiative is defeated (according to estimates by the Legislative Analyst’s Office). That’s an increase — and a very large one, at that.
Finally, the measure would continue the trend in which “temporary” taxes in California never seem to go away. As the proponents of Proposition 40 are discovering, voters are extremely distrustful of taxes described as temporary. Why? In large part because of Proposition 3 and its predecessor, Proposition 55 of 2016, asking voters to renew a tax originally described as a temporary charge to cover an emergency.
The ballot argument for the original initiative, Proposition 30 of 2012, said the taxes “are temporary, balanced and necessary to protect schools and safety” — one of the argument’s five mentions of the allegedly temporary nature.
With revenue arriving above projections and the state spending billions on questionable programs without proper controls or a review of effectiveness, it can no longer be said that California has a fiscal emergency.
The voters should give much-needed relief to small businesses and their customers, avoid making fiscal decisions prematurely, and let the “emergency tax” expire on schedule. Vote NO on Proposition 3.
•••
Robert Gutierrez is president of the California Taxpayers Association (https://caltax.org/), which is celebrating its 100th year of serving as the state’s largest and oldest association representing taxpayers in this state.

Proposition 3: Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care
Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

Pro Con
Proponents of Proposition 3 believe that the continuation of higher tax requirements on high-income earners is a crucial investment in students, communities, and educators. They maintain that the general population are demonstrably angry about income inequality and that failure to pass the proposition amounts to a tax cut for wealthy Californians.
Opponents argue that permanently extending the higher rates could encourage wealthy residents and businesses to leave California, potentially affecting jobs and economic growth. They also contend that making the rates permanent would make the policy harder to change in the future.

These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

Arguments for voting yes include preserving roughly $5 to $15 billion in annual revenue that schools and health care have come to depend on. The measure does not raise current taxes for most people and would prevent a tax cut for the top two percent. It is progressive because it targets high earners who have seen large income gains. California still spends relatively little on education despite rising costs. Expiration would create a fiscal cliff in 2031 forcing cuts to education or health. The proposal also includes accountability measures such as audits and criminal penalties.

The measure also supports the rainy day fund via Prop 2. Federal cuts may increase state fiscal pressure. Tax thresholds are indexed to inflation. Education spending rose significantly after Prop 30, and LCFF equity reforms were funded by this revenue. The top two percent already pay about half of all income taxes but capture disproportionate income and capital gains. Research shows education spending improves outcomes for low-income students. California has high inequality, which supports progressive taxation.

Arguments against the measure include breaking prior voter promises. The taxes were originally temporary in 2012 and 2016, so making them permanent removes future review. California already has the highest state income tax rate in the country. There is also credible research suggesting high taxes may drive high-income taxpayers and businesses out of the state.

Research on tax migration is mixed. Stanford, Rauh Hoover, IRS SOI data, and Zucman present conflicting findings.

Permanent high rates on volatile capital gains income would lock in boom-bust budgeting. The LAO itself notes swings of $5 to $15 billion annually.

Much of the revenue may have funded pension costs rather than classroom instruction. This needs verification.

Student outcomes show little improvement. NAEP scores, chronic absenteeism, and proficiency rates remain flat or decline despite spending increases.

California projects a loss of roughly 710,000 students between 2026 and 2036. Per-pupil funding could rise even without this tax if total funding stays flat.

Locking in the measure five years before expiration is risky. Fiscal conditions, federal policy, and potential wealth taxes like Prop 40 could shift the landscape by then.

Pass-through businesses such as S corporations, partnerships, and sole proprietors pay personal income tax. The surcharge would therefore affect some small and medium businesses, not just millionaires and billionaires.

The $371,000 single threshold captures many professionals and small business owners, not just billionaires. Campaign claims overstate the tax's impact.

State spending has grown far faster than population and inflation. The General Fund rose from roughly $90 billion in 2012 to about $250 billion today. This raises concerns about fiscal discipline.

A surplus of approximately $100 billion was spent down into deficits. That reflects a governance problem.

Locking in this revenue would enable continued expansion of programs like Medi-Cal for undocumented immigrants without requiring tradeoffs.

The claim that this is not a tax increase is misleading. Under current law the surcharges expire in 2031, so making them permanent would raise taxes relative to the existing schedule. The Attorney General and Legislative Analyst's Office confirm this.

Sunset provisions are sound policy because they force reevaluation. Permanent constitutional tax rates are difficult to reverse.

Post-pandemic tech and finance talent mobility has increased. Remote work makes residence more elastic, which could amplify any out-migration risk from high taxes.

PROP 3: The Permanent High-Income Tax Initiative
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%203.pdf)

California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 3 would take the Prop 30 higher personal income tax rates on top earners and make them permanent. Voters approved Prop 30 as a temporary measure in 2012 to close a budget shortfall. The measure was then extended in 2016 under Prop 55. Under current law the increased taxes expire after the 2030 tax year, so a yes vote is, in effect, a tax increase from 2031 onward compared with the law as it now stands. Hoover Institution research on the 2012 rate increase found that high earners’ responses to the higher tax rates, either by leaving the state or reporting less income, erased much of the revenue the higher rates were expected to raise.
Other Hoover Institution research shows that California’s budget already depends to an unusual degree on a small, mobile group of taxpayers whose income tends to be dependent on stock market performance. It also finds that much of the money raised for schools has been absorbed by rising pension costs rather than reaching classrooms.
Proposition 3 would enshrine into the state constitution increased fiscal dependence on a variable tax with no future date for voters to revisit the decision.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0016).
Type: Initiative constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: The temporary higher personal income tax rates on top earners become permanent instead of expiring after the 2030 tax year. Taxable income above about $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers (2025 tax brackets, adjusted annually for inflation) would continue to face marginal rates of 10.3 to 12.3 percent and of 13.3 percent on income above $1 million.
A vote NO means: The higher tax rates expire on schedule. Beginning in 2031, the top rate would return to 9.3 percent (plus the separate 1 percent income tax surcharge on income above $1 million, for a combined top rate of 10.3 percent).
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0016, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf)
LAO analysis: Proposition 3, Legislative Analyst’s Office (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 3 would remove the expiration date on the higher personal income tax rates that California voters first approved as Proposition 30 in 2012. These temporary taxes were intended to forestall additional education budget cuts in the wake of tax revenue declines following the Great Recession. They were set to expire after 2018, but Proposition 55 in 2016 extended the taxes through 2030 and added the formula for the taxes to fund Medi-Cal when revenues exceed specific benchmarks.
Now Prop 3 would make these taxes—1, 2, and 3 percentage point surcharges on top of the state’s 9.3 percent bracket—permanent. Combined with the separate 1 percent surcharge tax on personal income above $1 million (created by Proposition 63 in 2004), the Prop 30 income tax surcharges give California the highest top marginal personal income tax rate in the nation, at 13.3 percent. This rises further to 14.6 percent on wage income once the now-uncapped state disability insurance payroll tax is included.
These income tax surcharges fall on roughly the top 2 percent of tax filers in any given year, a group that already pays about half of all state income taxes. Because much of their income comes from highly variable capital gains, stock options, and business sales, the Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) expects the revenue at stake to swing between about $5 billion in a weak year and $15 billion in a strong year.
Supporters stress that Proposition 3 does not raise anyone’s rate this year. That is true—but incomplete. Current law already schedules these rates to end after 2030, so the relevant comparison is not today’s tax bill but the one taxpayers would face in 2031. Measured against current law, a yes vote raises taxes on affected earners from that point forward, permanently. The LAO’s own description of a yes vote is that “an income tax increase on high-income earners” would become permanent.
Despite Prop 30 originally being advertised as necessary to avoid education funding cuts, the tax doesn’t provide as much additional state funding for schools as would be expected on the surface. The tax revenue flows into the state’s general fund and is held in the Education Protection Account (EPA), whereupon it is disbursed to schools (89 percent) and community colleges (11 percent). However, because the EPA counts as general fund revenue, and Prop 98 only mandates (under the formula currently in effect) that about 40 percent of the general fund goes to education, only about 40 percent of Prop 30’s tax revenue actually represents an increase to school funding. Except for special circumstances, the remaining 60 percent of the EPA doesn’t necessarily increase school-related expenditures because those dollars count toward the Prop 98 guarantee. This means that policymakers can use the funding to replace other obligatory general fund education expenditures on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
In years when the state’s general fund revenues exceed both the Proposition 98 education spending guarantee and the cost of maintaining existing state programs, half of the excess (up to $2 billion, as stipulated by Prop 55) goes to Medi-Cal health services. The remainder supports other general fund programs and budget reserves. In summary, what was initially framed as a temporary tax to avoid cuts to education funding has shifted to effectively become ordinary California tax revenue and is poised to become permanent.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0016, “The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0016%20%28%26quot%3BThe%20California%20Children%26%23039%3Bs%20Education%20and%20Health%20Care%20Protection%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (filed August 29, 2025).
Key language:
The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date for the higher tax brackets.
What it amends: Section 36 of Article XIII of the California Constitution, the section created by Proposition 30 and extended by Proposition 55. Because the change is constitutional, the legislature cannot repeal or reduce the rates—only another statewide vote could change the tax rates.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
A permanent extension of the 1, 2, and 3 percentage point personal income tax surcharges on high earners, which would otherwise expire after the 2030 tax year.
Where?
Statewide, written into the state constitution at Article XIII, Section 36.
When?
On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the rates never expire. If it fails, the last tax year of the higher rates is 2030.
Why?
The measure’s sponsors, led by the California Teachers Association, frame making the tax permanent as protecting school and children’s healthcare funding from what would otherwise be a revenue loss. Opponents, led by the California Taxpayers Association, argue that Californians already pay among the nation’s highest taxes and that Sacramento should fix its excessive spending before making temporary taxes permanent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
The LAO’s estimate that the Prop 30 income tax surcharge is worth from $5 billion to $15 billion in revenue is effectively a static figure: It assumes that high earners keep living, working, and reporting income in California exactly as they would without the tax. Hoover Institution research examines this assumption directly. Using the full dataset of California tax returns, Hoover Senior Fellow Joshua D. Rauh and coauthor Ryan Shyu studied what happened after Proposition 30 raised top rates in 2012—0.8 percent more of the top-bracket tax base left the state in 2013 than otherwise would have been expected without the tax change. Moreover, the high earners who stayed reported substantially less taxable income; counterintuitively, this was actually the larger effect. Together, these responses erased 45.2 percent of the expected revenue gain in the first year and 60.9 percent of the total gain within the first two years.
A companion Hoover analysis noted that the 2017 federal tax reform which created a cap on state and local tax deductions hit high-income Californians with a force equivalent to 82 percent of another Proposition 30 tax increase. It suggested that the state was likely on the wrong side of the Laffer curve, meaning that increasing the top income tax rates was actually reducing the total tax revenue collected.
Similarly, in an October 2026 op-ed on Proposition 3 itself, Rauh and Hoover fellow Gregory Kearney argue that the top-bracket tax rates are now money losers for California. Before the 2017 cap on state and local tax deductions, high-income Californians could deduct much of their state tax bill on their federal returns. This had the effect of softening the impact of the income tax surcharges. Once the cap took effect, the surcharges imposed by Prop 30 began bearing close to their full weight on the state’s high-income households, which sharpened the incentive to move or restructure income. By the authors’ estimates, since 2018 the state has been losing more tax revenue from departing taxpayers or erosion of the tax base than it collects from those that remain.
Supporters of Prop 3 reply that high earners have not fled California, pointing to studies that find modest migration among millionaires. But Rauh’s earlier findings show why that reply misses the point: Departures accounted for less than a tenth of the lost revenue. Most of the erosion came from taxpayers who stayed and reported less income. This could have occurred by realizing fewer capital gains, shifting business activity to other taxing jurisdictions, or simply working less (or perhaps accepting other forms of income). Effectively, Prop 30 has provided a textbook example of how a tax base can shrink without anyone moving away.
Proposition 3 would also enshrine a revenue structure that Hoover research identifies as a major source of California’s fiscal instability. Hoover Senior Fellow Lee E. Ohanian shows that the top 1 percent of California households now provides roughly 40 to 50 percent of all personal income tax revenue and that the top 10 percent pay almost 90 percent. Because high-earning households tend to receive a large portion of their income from the stock market, which is highly variable, California’s personal income tax revenue surged by 55 percent in 2021 and then fell nearly 35 percent in 2023.
This feast-or-famine paradigm creates complications for funding ongoing programs and exposes California to revenue risk that it has little control over. Rauh and coauthor Jillian Ludwig describe this fragility as “baked into the system” and recommend steering more capital gains revenue into reserves rather than ongoing spending. Proposition 3 does the opposite: It treats the most volatile revenue in the state as a permanent foundation for ongoing commitments.
Moreover, the phrase “the top 2 percent of tax filers” somewhat misrepresents who pays the Prop 30 income tax surcharges. This is because those who pay the tax are not solely a group of consistent high earners. Some Californians would cross the relevant tax threshold only in the year they sell a home they have owned for decades or a small business they built. Capital gains from home sales are taxable when they exceed the home-sale exclusion of $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for joint filers. Citing a 2025 Redfin analysis, Rauh and Kearney note that 62 percent of California homes have appreciated at least $250,000 in value over their last sale price, and 33 percent had appreciated by at least $500,000. This suggests that a sizable share of California homeowners would see large one-time gains that could push them into the surcharge brackets in the year they sell. Owners of pass-through businesses, who report business profits on their personal returns, would also face these surcharges in successful years or years where they sell their businesses.
The biggest argument made in favor of Proposition 3 is premised on public schools not losing existing funding. However, Hoover research raises the question of where the increased funding has actually gone. By Rauh and Kearney’s calculations, the annual pension contributions for California’s K–12 school districts almost tripled between 2015 and 2023 to about $13 billion (excluding teachers’ own contributions). Over that period, the share of school employee spending devoted to pensions nearly doubled, from about 7 percent to more than 13 percent. If school districts had held pension costs at their 2015 share, Rauh and Kearney estimate, nearly $6 billion more would have been available for other education priorities last year alone. In other words, Prop 30’s income tax surcharges appear to a large extent to be funding increased retirement benefits.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 3 would turn a tax that voters were told was temporary into a permanent feature of the California Constitution. Compared with current law, it raises taxes on high earners from 2031 onward. Hoover Institution research suggests the revenue it protects is considerably smaller than the official estimate because the state’s most mobile taxpayers respond to higher rates by leaving or by reporting less income. It would also lock in California’s reliance on a narrow and volatile tax base while doing nothing to address the pension costs that have absorbed much of the money raised in the name of schools.

Story Title:
Proposition 3: California doesn’t need another forever tax
October 28, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/voting10.jpg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/commentary-vote-no-proposition-3/769223). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Proposition 3 asks voters to approve a massive tax increase that would not take effect until 2031, when California’s finances may look completely different from how they do today. Voters should reject Proposition 3 and keep their options open.
In 2031, there will be a new president in the Oval Office, a new governor, and a different political landscape in California — especially if voters approve Proposition 40 to impose a wealth tax that could prompt an exodus of the taxpayers targeted by Proposition 3.
Related Reading
CommentaryProposition 3 would help lock in hard-won resources for student well-being (https://edsource.org/2026/proposition-3-california-schools/769155) October 28, 2026
The state also will have significantly fewer students in our public schools. The Department of Finance projects a decline of 710,500 students from 2026 through 2036, and by the midpoint of this decline, we undoubtedly will see some major changes in the education structure.
This is only the beginning of the list of unknowns. Other questions include:
Will Californians still be paying billions of dollars per year for a nonfunctioning “high-speed” railroad system in 2031, rather than prioritizing schools for that spending?
Will taxpayers still be paying for ineffective programs that haven’t solved homelessness?
Will startups launch in California, or take their jobs and economic benefits to states with more competitive tax rates?
In short, it makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
What difference could five years make?
California’s finances can change substantially in a short period. Total state revenue for the current fiscal year is projected to be $21.5 billion higher than the amount collected five years earlier. The Department of Finance also recently reported that general fund revenue was running $5.5 billion above the projection used to draft the 2026-27 budget just six months earlier. This means the education funding guarantee will go up, too.
It makes no sense to amend the state constitution to commit to a tax increase now, five years in advance, when we have no idea what condition the state will be in when the tax would take effect.
Timing is only one of the problems. While Proposition 3 is marketed as a “tax extension” that would only affect high-income residents, the truth is that it’s a major tax increase that would hit millions of small businesses as well as high-income individuals. The result: California’s affordability crisis gets worse.
The small-business aspect of Proposition 3 hasn’t received enough attention. California’s tax structure does not neatly separate business income from personal income, and many small businesses operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships, or S corporations that report business earnings on personal income tax returns.
This means the higher tax rates imposed by Proposition 3 would increase taxes on many small businesses, ultimately leading to higher prices for customers, fewer job opportunities for workers, or both.
ThePublic Policy Institute of California reported in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-businesses/) that sole proprietorships accounted for more than 3 million California businesses in 2023. But the number of those businesses whose owners would be impacted by Proposition 3 depends on their taxable income.
To the extent that Proposition 3 would hit high-income earners, it would make California more reliant on the most volatile source of revenue, while simultaneously making it even more volatile by giving high-income residents a new incentive to leave the state.
California already imposes the nation’s highest personal income taxes and would have a top personal income tax rate of 10.3% on income over $1 million without Proposition 3. The state also imposes a 1.3% State Disability Insurance tax on all income from salaries and wages, bringing the top tax rate to 11.6% on those forms of income, without Proposition 3.
As for the issue of an “extension” versus an “increase,” the fact is clear: If Proposition 3 is approved, Californians will pay $5 billion to $15 billion a year more in state income tax than if the initiative is defeated (according to estimates by the Legislative Analyst’s Office). That’s an increase — and a very large one, at that.
Finally, the measure would continue the trend in which “temporary” taxes in California never seem to go away. As the proponents of Proposition 40 are discovering, voters are extremely distrustful of taxes described as temporary. Why? In large part because of Proposition 3 and its predecessor, Proposition 55 of 2016, asking voters to renew a tax originally described as a temporary charge to cover an emergency.
The ballot argument for the original initiative, Proposition 30 of 2012, said the taxes “are temporary, balanced and necessary to protect schools and safety” — one of the argument’s five mentions of the allegedly temporary nature.
With revenue arriving above projections and the state spending billions on questionable programs without proper controls or a review of effectiveness, it can no longer be said that California has a fiscal emergency.
The voters should give much-needed relief to small businesses and their customers, avoid making fiscal decisions prematurely, and let the “emergency tax” expire on schedule. Vote NO on Proposition 3.

Robert Gutierrez is president of the California Taxpayers Association (https://caltax.org/), which is celebrating its 100th year of serving as the state’s largest and oldest association representing taxpayers in this state.

Proposition 3: Provides Permanent Funding For Schools and Health Care By Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
High-Income Tax, Renew State Income Tax Increase for Education Funding Initiative
The California Children's Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026
Summary
Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering. 874,641 valid signatures were required. The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents. These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-6-2012-general-election-summary/november-6) in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-8-2016-general-election-summary/november-8-2) through 2030. Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent. Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets. The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 3 would maintain an estimated $5 billion to $15 billion in annual state revenue that would otherwise disappear when the higher income tax rates expire after 2030. The amount collected would vary from year to year because earnings among high-income taxpayers are especially sensitive to changes in the economy and stock market. Roughly 40 percent of the additional revenue would support K–12 schools and community colleges, while most of the remainder would be available for other General Fund programs and state reserves.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote would permanently continue California’s higher income tax rates of 10.3% to 12.3% on high-income earners, with the resulting education funding divided between K–12 schools (89%) and community colleges (11%).
NO: A “no” vote would leave current law unchanged, allowing these higher tax rates to expire in 2031.

Pro Con
Proponents of Proposition 3 believe that the continuation of higher tax requirements on high-income earners is a crucial investment in students, communities, and educators. They maintain that the general population are demonstrably angry about income inequality and that failure to pass the proposition amounts to a tax cut for wealthy Californians.
Opponents argue that permanently extending the higher rates could encourage wealthy residents and businesses to leave California, potentially affecting jobs and economic growth. They also contend that making the rates permanent would make the policy harder to change in the future.

- Joshua Rauh
- Ryan Shyu
American Economic Journal: Economic Policy
vol. 16, no. 1, February 2024
(pp. 34–86)
- Article Information
#### Abstract
Using administrative data, we analyze the response to Proposition 30, a 2012 measure that increased California marginal tax rates by up to 3 percentage points for high-income households.
Relative to baseline departure rates, an additional 0.8 percent of the residential tax base that landed in the top bracket left California in 2013.
Using matched out-of-state taxpayers as controls reveals an income elasticity with respect to the marginal net-of-tax rate of 2.5–3.2 for high earners who stayed.
These responses eroded 45.2 percent of state windfall tax revenues within the first year and 60.9 percent within 2 years, driven largely by the intensive margin.

# California’s High Taxes Are Driving The Wealthy Away
Yet California — whose economy is bigger than that of both countries — has comparable tax rates, when federal and state tolls are combined, and a new study suggests that they are causing some top earners to leave the state entirely [Joshua Rauh (Stanford; Google Scholar) & Ryan Shyu (Stanford), Behavioral Responses to State Income Taxation of High Earners: Evidence from California, 16 Amer. Econ. J. 34 (Feb. 2024)].
...
And higher taxes are playing a role.
Researchers Joshua Rauh and Ryan Shyu, currently and formerly at Stanford business school, have studied the behavioral response to Proposition 30, which boosted California’s marginal tax rates by up to 3% for high earners for seven years, from 2012 to 2018.
They found that in 2013, an additional 0.8% of the top bracket of the residential tax base left the state.
That is several times higher than the tax responses usually seen in the data.
These high-earning California residents seem to have reached a tipping point: Maybe many of them could afford the extra tax burden, but at some point they got fed up, read the signals and decided the broader system wasn’t working in their interest.

I am preparing to research the proposition and form a judgment.

I am weighing education outcomes, budget projections, and pension costs. I am also checking whether a NO vote would expire the tax in 2031.

A NO vote would not permanently block renewal; voters could re-approve the tax later. The real cost is the constitutional permanence commitment. I am also checking how Prop 40 might interact with this measure.

I am evaluating Prop 3 on its own merits. The tax was sold as temporary twice, so locking it in permanently removes the sunset that forces periodic review. A NO vote would not cut taxes until 2031; voters could still extend the measure later if the fiscal need is real.

Locking the tax in now destroys option value while enrollment is falling and federal policy is unstable. A simultaneous wealth tax could also create double taxation.

The best California-specific study shows the Prop 30 rate increase eroded 45 to 61 percent of expected revenue within two years. Elasticities of 2.5 to 3.2 indicate large behavioral responses.

Hoover's claim that the tax is a net revenue loser is speculative. The LAO still estimates $5 to $15 billion in static revenue, and the tax has raised over $100 billion cumulatively, so it is not a pure Laffer failure. Still, behavioral responses mean the LAO's static estimate likely overstates net revenue. Even at 40 to 60 percent erosion, billions remain.

The top one percent pay roughly half of all personal income tax.

Making the most volatile slice of revenue permanent as a base for ongoing programs is poor fiscal architecture. California has repeatedly spent windfalls and then cut, so locking in this volatility risks treating it as structural revenue.

The campaign claims all new revenue goes to classrooms. The LAO estimates only about forty percent of net new funds actually reach K-14 education; the rest substitutes for other general fund obligations or funds other programs.

Health care funding is indirect and only guaranteed through the Prop 55 Medi-Cal formula when a surplus exists.

District pension contributions rose by roughly six to eight billion dollars relative to their 2015 share. A large portion of new school revenue therefore went to pensions rather than instruction. More revenue without pension reform or spending restraint will yield diminishing returns for classrooms.

California NAEP scores have not improved commensurate with the substantial rise in real per-pupil spending since 2013.

Declining enrollment means the same total revenue buys higher per-pupil funding. A fiscal cliff is therefore less severe than it would otherwise be.

Prop 98 uses different formulas depending on the year. It can be based on student count or general fund revenue. This means declining enrollment does not automatically guarantee cuts to per-pupil spending.

The tax applies to households with taxable income above roughly $371,000 for singles and $742,000 for married couples. That threshold captures successful professionals, two-earner couples in coastal California, small business owners, and homeowners with large capital gains. In high-cost areas, this is affluent but not billionaire status.

The 10.3 percent surcharge begins at roughly $371,000 for singles and $742,000 for married couples. Higher brackets start even higher.

Combined federal, state, and SDI rates already reach about 13.3 percent for top earners. The effective marginal rate is very high.

High marginal rates distort work, investment location, and realization decisions.

General fund spending has grown from roughly ninety billion dollars to two hundred thirty to two hundred fifty billion dollars while population has remained flat. Real per capita spending has risen sharply. The claim that California faces only a revenue problem is weak; the state has both high needs and a spending discipline problem.

Structural dependence on the tax is real. Eight to twelve billion dollars per year is now baked into school budgets, Medi-Cal, and reserves. A sudden expiration in 2031 would force cuts, but a NO vote delays that hole until then and gives four years to adjust spending or pass a better tax.

The burden falls on the top two percent, who captured most income growth. California has high inequality.

State-level tax elasticities are higher than national ones because of mobility. Rauh's elasticity estimate suggests California may already be near or past the revenue-maximizing rate for the top bracket. This undermines the argument that raising taxes on the wealthy is easy revenue.

The Learning Policy Institute and other groups argue California still underspends on education relative to adequacy costs given high wages, high poverty rates among students, and English learner enrollment.

Jackson et al. find that sustained school spending increases improve outcomes, especially for poor students. California’s Local Control Funding Formula was a genuine equity reform enabled by Prop 30 revenue, so losing the tax could unwind supplemental and concentration grants.

Young et al. find only small migration effects from the tax. California still retains its concentration of high earners, IPOs, and venture capital a decade after Prop 30 passed. The tax has raised roughly one hundred four billion dollars in gross revenue.

Billionaire flight narratives typically target wealth taxes rather than the existing income tax. Because Prop 3 does not raise current rates, migration responses to permanence should be smaller than those to the original increase. People who were already leaving have largely already adjusted. The relevant question is the response to a rate that would fall in 2031 versus remaining fixed.

If tax elasticities are symmetric, letting rates fall in 2031 could increase reported income and in-migration, partially offsetting revenue loss. That would shrink the net fiscal gap below the LAO's static estimate of five to fifteen billion dollars. The cost of a NO vote may therefore be overstated.

Medi-Cal covers a large share of Californians. Federal cuts in 2026 would raise the state's share of health care costs, so maintaining revenue protects coverage.

The measure does not constitutionally dedicate most revenue to health care. The legislature could spend the freed general fund on anything.

Existing Prop 30 and Prop 55 audits and restrictions already govern the backfilled portion. New criminal penalties for misuse are largely redundant, since spending quality is the real constraint.

The temporary label is questionable. Many taxes begin as temporary, and the income tax piece was already extended once. A second extension to permanence is a deliberate policy choice rather than a continuation of an emergency. If services are ongoing, a permanent tax is more honest than serial sunset clauses. The counter is that sunsets provide leverage over a legislature that refuses to cut spending; permanence removes that leverage forever.

The better vote is no. The tax does not expire until after 2030, so voting no preserves the status quo through that year and keeps the option to extend later if budgets show a genuine structural gap.

The revenue case is overstated and the allocation case misleading. The LAO estimates that only about forty percent of the tax would be net new school funding. Campaign claims that Sacramento cannot touch the money are legally true of the EPA deposit but economically misleading because Prop 98 supplantation means the state can still use those funds. Health care funding is not a hard constitutional guarantee.

Rauh and Shyu 2024 show this exact tax erased most of its revenue windfall within two years through behavioral responses. California already has the highest personal income tax rate in the country. A permanent lock-in of that top rate is therefore a poor revenue source.

SALT deduction limits further raise the marginal excess burden.

Real per-capita general fund spending has roughly doubled while population remained flat. Student enrollment is now declining.

Pension costs absorbed a large share of school revenue gains.

NAEP and proficiency data do not justify treating more revenue as the binding constraint versus governance, pension reform, or program effectiveness.

A constitutional revenue lock-in would reduce pressure to fix those underlying problems.

The tax burden extends beyond millionaires and billionaires. Pass-through business income, professional couples, and one-time home or business sale gains also face the surcharge. Embedding the highest marginal rates permanently would worsen California’s cost-of-living and business-climate problems, hurting job creation and prices. The top two percent already pay about half of all personal income tax; further concentration increases fiscal fragility.

A NO vote preserves the money for four more years. That window allows a deliberate glide path, pension reform, or a broader tax design rather than locking in a volatile top-rate tax permanently.

The argument that California still underspends on education is taken seriously but not decisive. The real constraint is how funds are spent—pensions, administration, absenteeism, and curriculum—not just the total amount.

Per-pupil funding would rise as enrollment declines even if total revenue stays flat. Painful cuts in 2031 are a reason to plan rather than to lock in a tax permanently in 2026. A no vote would give future high earners a tax cut relative to today, but those earners have already paid the surcharge for fourteen to nineteen years by then. The original agreement was temporary. Progressive taxation can still be maintained at the existing top rate of ten point three percent.
The revenue mechanics and the behavioral evidence are the crux. I’ll check the operative text, school results, and nonpartisan budget context before deciding.
