The tax applies to households with taxable income above roughly $371,000 for singles and $742,000 for married couples. That threshold captures successful professionals, two-earner couples in coastal California, small business owners, and homeowners with large capital gains. In high-cost areas, this is affluent but not billionaire status.

The 10.3 percent surcharge begins at roughly $371,000 for singles and $742,000 for married couples. Higher brackets start even higher.

Combined federal, state, and SDI rates already reach about 13.3 percent for top earners. The effective marginal rate is very high.

High marginal rates distort work, investment location, and realization decisions.

General fund spending has grown from roughly ninety billion dollars to two hundred thirty to two hundred fifty billion dollars while population has remained flat. Real per capita spending has risen sharply. The claim that California faces only a revenue problem is weak; the state has both high needs and a spending discipline problem.

Structural dependence on the tax is real. Eight to twelve billion dollars per year is now baked into school budgets, Medi-Cal, and reserves. A sudden expiration in 2031 would force cuts, but a NO vote delays that hole until then and gives four years to adjust spending or pass a better tax.

The burden falls on the top two percent, who captured most income growth. California has high inequality.

State-level tax elasticities are higher than national ones because of mobility. Rauh's elasticity estimate suggests California may already be near or past the revenue-maximizing rate for the top bracket. This undermines the argument that raising taxes on the wealthy is easy revenue.

The Learning Policy Institute and other groups argue California still underspends on education relative to adequacy costs given high wages, high poverty rates among students, and English learner enrollment.

Jackson et al. find that sustained school spending increases improve outcomes, especially for poor students. California’s Local Control Funding Formula was a genuine equity reform enabled by Prop 30 revenue, so losing the tax could unwind supplemental and concentration grants.

Young et al. find only small migration effects from the tax. California still retains its concentration of high earners, IPOs, and venture capital a decade after Prop 30 passed. The tax has raised roughly one hundred four billion dollars in gross revenue.

Billionaire flight narratives typically target wealth taxes rather than the existing income tax. Because Prop 3 does not raise current rates, migration responses to permanence should be smaller than those to the original increase. People who were already leaving have largely already adjusted. The relevant question is the response to a rate that would fall in 2031 versus remaining fixed.

If tax elasticities are symmetric, letting rates fall in 2031 could increase reported income and in-migration, partially offsetting revenue loss. That would shrink the net fiscal gap below the LAO's static estimate of five to fifteen billion dollars. The cost of a NO vote may therefore be overstated.

Medi-Cal covers a large share of Californians. Federal cuts in 2026 would raise the state's share of health care costs, so maintaining revenue protects coverage.

The measure does not constitutionally dedicate most revenue to health care. The legislature could spend the freed general fund on anything.

Existing Prop 30 and Prop 55 audits and restrictions already govern the backfilled portion. New criminal penalties for misuse are largely redundant, since spending quality is the real constraint.

The temporary label is questionable. Many taxes begin as temporary, and the income tax piece was already extended once. A second extension to permanence is a deliberate policy choice rather than a continuation of an emergency. If services are ongoing, a permanent tax is more honest than serial sunset clauses. The counter is that sunsets provide leverage over a legislature that refuses to cut spending; permanence removes that leverage forever.

The better vote is no. The tax does not expire until after 2030, so voting no preserves the status quo through that year and keeps the option to extend later if budgets show a genuine structural gap.

The revenue case is overstated and the allocation case misleading. The LAO estimates that only about forty percent of the tax would be net new school funding. Campaign claims that Sacramento cannot touch the money are legally true of the EPA deposit but economically misleading because Prop 98 supplantation means the state can still use those funds. Health care funding is not a hard constitutional guarantee.

Rauh and Shyu 2024 show this exact tax erased most of its revenue windfall within two years through behavioral responses. California already has the highest personal income tax rate in the country. A permanent lock-in of that top rate is therefore a poor revenue source.

SALT deduction limits further raise the marginal excess burden.

Real per-capita general fund spending has roughly doubled while population remained flat. Student enrollment is now declining.

Pension costs absorbed a large share of school revenue gains.

NAEP and proficiency data do not justify treating more revenue as the binding constraint versus governance, pension reform, or program effectiveness.

A constitutional revenue lock-in would reduce pressure to fix those underlying problems.

The tax burden extends beyond millionaires and billionaires. Pass-through business income, professional couples, and one-time home or business sale gains also face the surcharge. Embedding the highest marginal rates permanently would worsen California’s cost-of-living and business-climate problems, hurting job creation and prices. The top two percent already pay about half of all personal income tax; further concentration increases fiscal fragility.

A NO vote preserves the money for four more years. That window allows a deliberate glide path, pension reform, or a broader tax design rather than locking in a volatile top-rate tax permanently.

The argument that California still underspends on education is taken seriously but not decisive. The real constraint is how funds are spent—pensions, administration, absenteeism, and curriculum—not just the total amount.

Per-pupil funding would rise as enrollment declines even if total revenue stays flat. Painful cuts in 2031 are a reason to plan rather than to lock in a tax permanently in 2026. A no vote would give future high earners a tax cut relative to today, but those earners have already paid the surcharge for fourteen to nineteen years by then. The original agreement was temporary. Progressive taxation can still be maintained at the existing top rate of ten point three percent.","format":"xai-responses-v1","index":0},{"type":"reasoning.encrypted","data":".eyJlbmRwb2ludF9zbHVnIjoieC1haS9ncm9rLTQuNy0yMDI2MDkxNnx4YWkifQ","format":"xai-responses-v1","id":"rs_25763379-19c5-94d7-b099-77692160410e","index":1}]

Should Voters Approve Prop. 3? How Top Tax Rates Have Helped Californians
A Look at What California's Top Tax Rates Have Funded — and What's at Risk if Voters Don't Approve Prop. 3
July 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 3 will appear on the November 2026 statewide ballot, asking California voters whether to make permanent the higher-income tax rates on the state’s highest earners. These top tax rates were first enacted by voters in 2012 and renewed in 2016 to help fund schools, health care, and other supports for working families. Without action, the current rates are set to expire after 2030, reducing state revenues by billions of dollars annually and threatening funding for schools and state programs and services that support Californians every day.

What Would Prop. 3 Do?
Prop. 3 would make permanent the rates put in place since 2012, preserving a key element of progressivity (requiring households with higher incomes to pay higher tax rates) in the state’s revenue structure that funds critical investments that improve the quality of life for all Californians. The measure would not raise taxes or change existing income tax rates; it simply removes the expiration date on current tax rates for the state’s highest earners. Revenues would continue to support the entire state General Fund budget by helping meet the TK-14 constitutional funding guarantee and freeing up revenue for other programs and services, just as they have since 2012.
Background on Prop. 30 and Prop. 55
In 2012, after the state faced significant revenue losses as a result of the Great Recession, California voters approved Proposition 30, which added new income tax brackets for the state’s highest earners (10.3%, 11.3%, and 12.3%, depending on household income) and included a temporary sales tax increase. Both the income tax rates and the sales tax increase were temporary, with the sales tax set to expire in 2016 and the income tax rates in 2018. Proposition 30 also created the Education Protection Account, a state account in the General Fund that receives and disburses revenues from the top income tax rates.
what is the education protection account (epa)?
Proposition 30 (2012) established the Education Protection Account, a state account where revenues from the top income tax rates are deposited. Of the funds in the account, 89% are distributed to schools and 11% to community colleges. This revenue is treated as General Fund revenue, subject to constitutional requirements including Prop. 98 (1988), the state’s minimum funding guarantee for TK-14 education, and Prop. 2 (2014), which established rules for building state budget reserves and paying down state debts. The revenue deposited into the EPA increases the Prop. 98 guarantee and is used to help meet the guarantee, freeing up General Fund revenue for other state budget priorities.
In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55, which extended the income tax rates for another 12 years (to 2030), while allowing the sales tax to expire as scheduled. Prop. 55 also added a constitutional formula intended to increase funding for the Medi-Cal program (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/3765) when revenues exceed a certain threshold. This specific formula has never directed funds to Medi-Cal, and the current measure would allow it to expire. However, top tax rate revenues do support the Medi-Cal budget indirectly through the General Fund capacity generated by Prop. 55.
Since their initial enactment in 2012, these higher tax rates have generated around $120 billion for schools and other essential services. In recent years, the higher rates have generated around $10 billion annually. These revenues now form a core component of the state budget, supporting the TK-14 education budget, strengthening General Fund capacity to support other vital programs and services, and building reserves.
Who Pays the Voter-Approved Top Tax Rates?
The voter-approved top tax rates only impact the highest-income Californians.
These rates only apply to the top 2% of California tax filers (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016). In tax year 2025, these top rates only applied to people with incomes above around $371,000 for single tax filers and about $743,000 for married couples filing jointly. These thresholds increase annually with inflation.
Without Voter-Approved Tax Rates, the Top 1% Would Receive Another Tax Cut
The top-earning 1% of Californians would receive a major tax cut if Prop. 55 rates are not extended. If the voter-approved top tax rates are allowed to expire, the vast majority of tax filers in the top 1% by income would receive an average annual tax cut of nearly $59,000, according to estimates from the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy. This top 1% group would get about 98% of the total tax cuts. The remaining tax cuts would go to some households in the next 4% of highest-income filers. 1 (javascript:void(0)) Not all households in the top 5% or top 1% would receive tax cuts from the expiration of the top tax rates for several reasons. First, filers are subject to the top tax rates if their taxable income — that is, income after accounting for allowed exemptions and deductions — exceeds the thresholds established by Prop. 30 and Prop. 50. In contrast, the thresholds for the top 5% and top 1% used by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy for this analysis are based on total income before exemptions and deductions. So tax filers in the top 1% by total income may have taxable incomes under the threshold for the top rates. Second, some high-income filers that use specific tax preferences may be subject to an “alternative minimum tax,” which could be triggered if their regular tax bill were reduced. And finally, because thresholds for these rates vary by household type, a married couple filing a joint tax return with a total income of $500,000 falls into the top 5% of all tax filers, but their total income — even before accounting for exemptions and deductions — is below the threshold for the Prop. 55 taxes of around $743,000, for example. Around 15% of this group would receive a tax cut, averaging more than $2,000 annually. Californians in all other income groups would see no change to their taxes.
California’s tax system would be more regressive if the Prop. 55 tax rates expire. A regressive tax system (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-tax-revenue-system-isnt-fair-for-all/) is one in which lower-income households pay larger shares of their income in taxes than higher-income households. In contrast, in a progressive tax system, higher-income people pay higher shares of their income in taxes. California’s tax system is more progressive than many other state tax systems (https://itep.org/whopays-7th-edition/), in large part due to these voter-approved top tax rates that are up for renewal under Prop. 3.
When you add up the various state and local taxes that Californians pay — including the sales tax, property tax, and other types of taxes — the highest-income 1% currently pay about 12% of their income in taxes on average. That’s barely more than the 11.7% paid by Californians in the lowest 20% by income. If the top rates were not in effect, the top 1% would pay only about 10.7% of their income in state and local taxes — lower than what the bottom fifth of Californians pay.
Top Earners’ Incomes Have Soared
The number of Californians with incomes high enough to be subject to the voter-approved top tax rates has more than doubled, reflecting soaring incomes among top earners. Around 185,000 tax filers, including more than 175,000 California resident filers, had incomes above the thresholds for Prop. 30’s top tax rates in 2013, the first year the rates were in effect. By 2024 (the latest available data), the number had reached nearly 376,000, including around 355,000 California residents. 2 (javascript:void(0)) “Tax filer” represents a tax filing unit — the primary filer as well as any spouses and dependents included on the tax return. A tax filing unit can be an individual, a couple, or a family, and in some cases can include unrelated dependents. This increase is due to the incomes of these high-income households growing much faster than inflation over this period.
Californians subject to the top tax rates have seen their incomes grow dramatically over the past several decades, while most Californians have lost ground or experienced income declines after adjusting for inflation . The top 1% of Californians saw their inflation-adjusted incomes increase more than 2.5 times (157%) between 1987 and 2024, while those in the bottom 80% saw decreases in real income over that time.
To be in the top 1%, a tax filer had an income of at least $973,097 in 2024. On average, this group reported more than $3 million per tax return in 2024 — about 54 times the income of the middle fifth of Californians, who earned around $56,000 on average. In even starker contrast, the top 0.1% had an average income of over $15 million — 268 times that of the middle fifth of Californians. In other words, someone in the top 1% can earn in just under one week what the average middle-income Californian earns in an entire year, and someone in the top 0.1% can earn that amount in just over a day .
What Have the Top Income Tax Rates Accomplished?
Since the passage of Prop. 30 in 2012, the top tax rates have generated about $120 billion in state revenue. 3 (javascript:void(0)) This figure reflects revenues from the top tax rates allocated to TK-14 education from the Education Protection Account (EPA) through the 2024-25 fiscal year. On average, this revenue has represented about 5.5% of total General Fund revenues. The funds raised by the top tax rates approved by voters through Prop. 30 and Prop. 55 have been a major revenue source for the state, supporting critical services including education, health care, and economic security programs. This revenue has also helped the state to build up budget reserves to be better prepared for downturns when revenues decline or come in lower than expected.
The annual revenue raised by the top tax rates has increased in line with overall state revenues . These revenues are sensitive to stock market fluctuations, as a large share of the income of high-income households comes from earnings on investments such as dividends and capital gains. For example, Prop. 55 revenues peaked at more than $16 billion when the stock market surged in 2021 and then subsequently fell in line with the stock market decline in the following years, before growing to nearly $12 billion in 2024. The sensitivity of these revenues to economic conditions makes it all the more important that state leaders have the capacity to save revenues during high-revenue years in the state’s budget reserves for future downturns, as required under Prop. 2 of 2014 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/app/uploads/140924_Proposition_2_BB.pdf)— which may be modified to require additional savings in some strong-revenue years if voters approve changes to the existing measure with Prop. 2 on the November 2026 ballot.
Top tax rate revenues provide critical support for schools and community colleges . Top tax rate revenues serve two purposes for the TK-14 education budget: 1) increase the Prop. 98 minimum guarantee’s annual calculation and 2) provide the revenues needed to meet the guarantee. Because top tax rate revenues count as General Fund revenues, they directly affect how the annual Prop. 98 level is calculated. In years when the General Fund experiences strong growth, the guarantee is set as a share (about 40%) of General Fund revenues, establishing a higher floor. 4 (javascript:void(0)) The minimum guarantee is determined using one of three formulas: 1) approximately 40% of General Fund revenue, 2) the prior year level adjusted for K-12 attendance growth and growth in per capita personal income, or 3) the prior year level adjusted for K-12 attendance growth and per capita General Fund revenue growth. In other years, the guarantee builds on the prior year’s level, carrying forward the growth built when revenues were strong. Regardless of how the guarantee is calculated, the effect of the top tax rate revenue is cumulative. As shown in the chart below, the guarantee has grown on an ongoing basis since 2012-13, with part of this growth attributable to the top tax rates.
what is proposition 98?
Prop. 98 is a constitutional amendment adopted by California voters in 1988 that establishes an annual minimum funding level for TK-14 education each fiscal year, commonly referred to as the minimum guarantee. Prop. 98 funding comes from a combination of state General Fund revenue and local property taxes. Prop. 98 spending supports TK-12 schools, community colleges, county offices of education, the state preschool program, and state agencies that provide direct TK-14 instructional programs. While Prop. 98 establishes a required minimum funding level for programs falling under the guarantee as a whole, it does not protect individual programs from reduction or elimination.
In addition to raising the guarantee’s calculation, Prop. 55 revenues directly help meet the guarantee. Revenues from the top tax rates are used to meet the Prop. 98 obligation, which frees up General Fund dollars that would otherwise be needed to meet the guarantee. These freed-up dollars are used to support non-TK-14 programs, build state reserves, and pay down debts. Since 2012-13, when these revenues began to flow to schools and community colleges, Prop. 55 revenues have provided about $120 billion to help meet the TK-14 budget. 5 (javascript:void(0)) While the top tax rate revenues have provided approximately $120 billion to the TK-14 budget through the EPA, because these revenues also reduce the General Fund dollars to meet the guarantee, the overall education funding impact is approximately 40% of total revenues.

An important finding from the CalBudget Center has been identified.

Prop 55's health care funding formula has never triggered. Prop 3 would let it expire. The health care benefit is indirect.

Prop 3 would keep the tax rates in place until 2031. The Medi-Cal formula has its own sunset date of December 2031. If the measure does not extend that date, the health care allocation would expire even though the taxes continue.

The PDF text extraction likely failed to preserve the strikeout and italic formatting. That distinction is critical for determining exactly what Prop 3 deletes versus keeps.

Hoover's analysis clarifies that Prop 3 removes the expiration date for higher tax brackets. The measure would make those rates permanent while allowing the Medi-Cal supplemental formula to expire without extension. The EPA education funding mechanism would likely continue indefinitely.

The campaign's argument that freed education funds will support health care is indirect and not guaranteed. The structural deficit of $8 to $35 billion annually already exists while the tax is in effect, so the surtax does not close it. Making the tax permanent would not resolve this pre-existing gap.

After 2031, the tax expiration would widen the structural deficit by $5 to $15 billion annually. The state would still need to cut spending or raise other revenue before that date regardless.

PPIC data shows California per-pupil spending is above the national average in nominal terms, but ranks 26th after labor cost adjustments. Pension contributions absorbed roughly 25 percent of pre-pandemic spending increases. LCFF funding for high-need students improved test scores somewhat.

Recent NAEP data shows California remains below average in many subjects despite spending increases. A 2024 national study found post-COVID declines, and California has historically lagged behind the rest of the country.

Rauh and Shyu provide credible peer-reviewed evidence of large behavioral responses to this tax.

Even critics of Rauh and Shyu agree that intensive margin effects matter. The elasticity estimates are high relative to the literature, and some economists worry that short-run income shifting overstates long-run elasticity. Still, the tax raised roughly $100 to $120 billion, so it was not a Laffer disaster in levels. The key question for permanence is whether keeping the extra one to three percentage points after 2031 would raise net revenue once behavioral responses are accounted for. The LAO static estimate is the official figure voters see.

Even if forty to sixty percent of the tax is lost to behavioral responses, roughly two to nine billion dollars in net revenue would remain. The excess burden per dollar raised is high because of the elasticity. The measure also contains a conflicting measures clause that would invalidate any other statewide personal income tax proposal on the same ballot.

The conflicting measures clause is a poison-pill provision. If Prop 3 wins by a wider margin than any other income-tax measure on the same ballot, that competing proposal is null and void. Prop 40 is a wealth tax, not an income tax. I am now checking whether any other personal income tax proposals appear on the November 2026 ballot.

## The 2018-19 Budget: The Administration’s Proposition 55 Estimates
**Description:** Proposition 55 (2016) aimed to increase funding for Medi-Cal under a formula administered by the Department of Finance.
In 2018-19, the first year of implementation of this calculation, the administration’s interpretations and estimates result in no additional funds to Medi-Cal.
Two key choices lead to this result.
First, the administration’s decision to subtract $3.5 billion from available revenues to account for its proposed optional reserve deposit significantly reduces the calculation’s starting point, eliminating a surplus that would have directed funds to Medi-Cal.
Second, the administration’s workload budget approach is based on a broad definition of currently authorized services, which also has the effect of reducing the amount of potential funds for Medi-Cal under the measure.
Different decisions about these two features of the measure could result in more or less funding for Medi-Cal by hundreds of millions—or even billions—of dollars in the future.

I have enough information to recommend a vote.

The answer is no. Locking in the highest state income tax rates into the constitution with no sunset is premature. The tax only expires after 2030, so a no vote preserves flexibility for four years when enrollment trends, structural deficits, and federal policy are clearer.

Undoing a yes vote would require another statewide election. The proposition converts the 2012 tax increase into permanent law five years early, despite the original promise of temporary taxes. Sunsets are the proper accountability mechanism when spending outpaces revenue.

The campaign claims every dollar goes to classrooms and healthcare. The LAO estimates only about 40 percent is new funding for schools and community colleges. The rest backfills the General Fund and other programs.

EPA dollars count toward Prop 98. They replace existing General Fund education spending dollar-for-dollar in typical years.

The Prop 55 Medi-Cal formula has never sent a dollar to Medi-Cal. The CalBudget Center says Prop 3 lets that formula expire.

Healthcare funding is an indirect claim about freed-up General Fund capacity. The legislature could spend that money on anything.

The "no administrative costs" promise applies only to EPA funds at districts. The remaining sixty percent is effectively general revenue. Districts can use EPA funds for teacher salaries, but this does not create a new accountability revolution.

California already faces multi-billion-dollar operating deficits before the surtax expires. Spending growth has outpaced revenue growth. Making a volatile tax permanent would not fix this structural imbalance. It would reduce pressure to align spending with a sustainable base and add another boom-bust revenue stream.

Prop 2 reserves have not prevented repeated deficit cycles after the 2021-22 windfall was spent.

Research on Prop 30 shows this tax eroded revenue sharply. A study using California tax returns found the one-to-three point increase cut expected revenue by forty-five percent in year one and sixty-one percent within two years. Most of that loss came from lower reported income, with elasticity estimates near two to three. A small migration effect also reduced the top-bracket tax base.

The LAO's $5-15 billion estimate assumes no behavioral response. Net revenue is still positive, but the excess burden per dollar is high. California already has the highest top rate in the country at 13.3 percent. Permanence would prevent the scheduled drop to a still-high 10.3 percent rate.

State-level tax elasticities are higher than federal ones because people and income can move. Locking in the rate most likely to be on the wrong side of the state Laffer curve is poor tax design.

The top one percent pay roughly half of all personal income tax. Much of that revenue comes from capital gains. Revenue swings sharply with market conditions, from about five billion dollars in weak years to fifteen billion dollars in strong years. Making this volatile slice a permanent foundation for schools and health is risky.

Per-pupil spending is now above the national average. California is no longer among the bottom ten states. The emergency that justified Prop 30 has passed.

Pension contributions nearly tripled and now absorb roughly a quarter of the pre-pandemic spending increase. That crowding out has reduced funds available for classrooms.

California's 2024 NAEP scores remain slightly below the national average. Gains from 2003 to 2019 largely predated or coincided with early Prop 30. Post-2019 progress stalled.

The LCFF did improve targeting and raised some test scores for high-need students. That is a real benefit of the revenue era.

Declining enrollment will raise per-pupil resources even if total revenue stays flat. A four-year window exists to resize the system before any cliff.

A 2031 cliff would be painful, but that calls for a glide path or a later extension. It does not justify pre-committing in 2026 on a misleading ballot title.

The tax applies to ordinary households too. Pass-through business income is taxed on personal returns, and one-time capital gains can push middle-class filers into the brackets for a year. The ITEP estimate that ninety-eight percent of the tax-cut-if-expire benefit goes to the top one percent is the strongest argument for yes.

The campaign's claim that only millionaires and billionaires pay this tax overstates the reality. Even after expiration, California would still have one of the most progressive state income tax systems in the country, with a 9.3 percent bracket and a separate 1 percent tax on income above one million dollars. ITEP also notes that combined state and local taxes on the top one percent are only marginally higher than those on the bottom quintile because of sales and excise regressivity. That makes preserving a progressive personal income tax a fairer argument for yes.

Prop 40 would tax the same narrow base as the income surtax. The LAO warns it could reduce ongoing income tax revenue through departure. Locking the surtax permanently in the same election while a one-time wealth tax might chase high earners out would compound fiscal risk.

Prop 3's conflicting-measures clause targets other personal income tax changes. Prop 40 is a separate asset tax, so the two may not legally conflict. Still, a no vote preserves the income-tax sunset as a safety valve if Prop 40 passes and triggers out-migration.

A no vote does not cut school funding in 2026 through 2030. It does not repeal LCFF. It does not reduce Medi-Cal now.

The campaign is pushing for a permanent vote now because it is easier to lock in before the 2031 cliff becomes visible and before voters see another temporary promise broken. A cleaner extension with a sunset, broader base, or reserve rules could be considered later if schools truly need the revenue. That timing argument favors a no vote.

A yes vote is defensible for those who prioritize avoiding the 2031 cliff, preserving progressive taxation, distrusting future renewals, and believing short-run elasticities will not persist. Those arguments are weaker than the case for no. The renewal option remains open, and the measure's health-care dedication is largely fictional.

The strongest argument for yes is that California already faces multi-billion-dollar structural deficits. Letting the surtax expire in 2031 would deepen an already unsustainable budget, and the political system has a history of cutting schools and health before other programs or using gimmicks. High earners have also seen their real income surge by over 157 percent since 1987 while the bottom eighty percent fell.

The tax has been paid for fourteen years without destroying the state economy. California remains a major innovation hub, and the $120 billion raised proves the static fears were overstated even if elasticities reduced the windfall. Schools recovered from the Great Recession and LCFF equity happened because of this revenue. A no vote is a bet that future voters and legislators will replace or resize the tax, but California's track record on fiscal responsibility is poor. Locking in the revenue may be the lesser evil.

A social-welfare lens suggests the tax would yield roughly two to three billion dollars annually for K-14 education, or several hundred dollars per pupil. Jackson and Lafortune/PPIC evidence indicates that money matters most for high-need students, and LCFF supplemental grants are valuable.

The campaign cites federal budget cuts that may reduce Medicaid funding. That would raise the value of state revenue for health care and safety-net programs.

A yes vote carries real costs. Elasticity estimates of two to three mean deadweight loss is large relative to revenue, though some of that elasticity reflects tax avoidance rather than pure resource loss. The migration of high earners would also create first-order fiscal externalities for the state. Locking the tax in permanently prevents future rate reductions if evidence of harm accumulates.

Locking in the surtax would encourage spending the volatile revenue on ongoing programs, worsening future fiscal crises. It would also reduce the likelihood of a better tax later, such as a broader base or a lower permanent rate with a sunset review.

A no vote would create a 2031 cliff of roughly five to fifteen billion dollars in static revenue, or four to eight billion after behavioral gains from rate reduction. That is manageable relative to the two hundred fifty billion general fund and existing structural deficits. The state will still need to cut over ten billion dollars in annual spending growth regardless.

The expiration would be an incremental adjustment rather than a catastrophic cliff if phased over four years. A future extension could also fail politically even if needed.

Voters have approved school taxes in 2012 and 2016. The risk of a future renewal failing is moderate, not extreme.

The recommendation is no. Constitutionalizing a temporary emergency tax as permanent five years before expiration is a poor institutional design choice. The health-care dedication is largely an accounting identity rather than new school funding. The health formula never worked and is being dropped. The state already faces structural deficits that this tax does not close. Enrollment is falling. Behavioral elasticities are high. Voters retain the option to extend the tax later.

Pension contributions nearly tripled and now absorb roughly a quarter of the pre-pandemic spending increase. That crowding out has reduced funds available for classrooms.

California's 2024 NAEP scores remain slightly below the national average. Gains from 2003 to 2019 largely predated or coincided with early Prop 30. Post-2019 progress stalled.

The LCFF did improve targeting and raised some test scores for high-need students. That is a real benefit of the revenue era.

Declining enrollment will raise per-pupil resources even if total revenue stays flat. A four-year window exists to resize the system before any cliff.

A 2031 cliff would be painful, but that calls for a glide path or a later extension. It does not justify pre-committing in 2026 on a misleading ballot title.

The tax applies to ordinary households too. Pass-through business income is taxed on personal returns, and one-time capital gains can push middle-class filers into the brackets for a year. The ITEP estimate that ninety-eight percent of the tax-cut-if-expire benefit goes to the top one percent is the strongest argument for yes.

The campaign's claim that only millionaires and billionaires pay this tax overstates the reality. Even after expiration, California would still have one of the most progressive state income tax systems in the country, with a 9.3 percent bracket and a separate 1 percent tax on income above one million dollars. ITEP also notes that combined state and local taxes on the top one percent are only marginally higher than those on the bottom quintile because of sales and excise regressivity. That makes preserving a progressive personal income tax a fairer argument for yes.

Prop 40 would tax the same narrow base as the income surtax. The LAO warns it could reduce ongoing income tax revenue through departure. Locking the surtax permanently in the same election while a one-time wealth tax might chase high earners out would compound fiscal risk.

Prop 3's conflicting-measures clause targets other personal income tax changes. Prop 40 is a separate asset tax, so the two may not legally conflict. Still, a no vote preserves the income-tax sunset as a safety valve if Prop 40 passes and triggers out-migration.

A no vote does not cut school funding in 2026 through 2030. It does not repeal LCFF. It does not reduce Medi-Cal now.

The campaign is pushing for a permanent vote now because it is easier to lock in before the 2031 cliff becomes visible and before voters see another temporary promise broken. A cleaner extension with a sunset, broader base, or reserve rules could be considered later if schools truly need the revenue. That timing argument favors a no vote.

A yes vote is defensible for those who prioritize avoiding the 2031 cliff, preserving progressive taxation, distrusting future renewals, and believing short-run elasticities will not persist. Those arguments are weaker than the case for no. The renewal option remains open, and the measure's health-care dedication is largely fictional.

The strongest argument for yes is that California already faces multi-billion-dollar structural deficits. Letting the surtax expire in 2031 would deepen an already unsustainable budget, and the political system has a history of cutting schools and health before other programs or using gimmicks. High earners have also seen their real income surge by over 157 percent since 1987 while the bottom eighty percent fell.

The tax has been paid for fourteen years without destroying the state economy. California remains a major innovation hub, and the $120 billion raised proves the static fears were overstated even if elasticities reduced the windfall. Schools recovered from the Great Recession and LCFF equity happened because of this revenue. A no vote is a bet that future voters and legislators will replace or resize the tax, but California's track record on fiscal responsibility is poor. Locking in the revenue may be the lesser evil.

A social-welfare lens suggests the tax would yield roughly two to three billion dollars annually for K-14 education, or several hundred dollars per pupil. Jackson and Lafortune/PPIC evidence indicates that money matters most for high-need students, and LCFF supplemental grants are valuable.

The campaign cites federal budget cuts that may reduce Medicaid funding. That would raise the value of state revenue for health care and safety-net programs.

A yes vote carries real costs. Elasticity estimates of two to three mean deadweight loss is large relative to revenue, though some of that elasticity reflects tax avoidance rather than pure resource loss. The migration of high earners would also create first-order fiscal externalities for the state. Locking the tax in permanently prevents future rate reductions if evidence of harm accumulates.

Locking in the surtax would encourage spending the volatile revenue on ongoing programs, worsening future fiscal crises. It would also reduce the likelihood of a better tax later, such as a broader base or a lower permanent rate with a sunset review.

A no vote would create a 2031 cliff of roughly five to fifteen billion dollars in static revenue, or four to eight billion after behavioral gains from rate reduction. That is manageable relative to the two hundred fifty billion general fund and existing structural deficits. The state will still need to cut over ten billion dollars in annual spending growth regardless.

The expiration would be an incremental adjustment rather than a catastrophic cliff if phased over four years. A future extension could also fail politically even if needed.

Voters have approved school taxes in 2012 and 2016. The risk of a future renewal failing is moderate, not extreme.

The recommendation is no. Constitutionalizing a temporary emergency tax as permanent five years before expiration is a poor institutional design choice. The health-care dedication is largely an accounting identity rather than new school funding. The health formula never worked and is being dropped. The state already faces structural deficits that this tax does not close. Enrollment is falling. Behavioral elasticities are high.
